# A World of Worlds

Somewhere on a twig at the edge of a forest path, a tick is waiting. She has been waiting for two years. She may wait for longer — there are laboratory records, cited by the biologist Jakob von Uexküll nearly a century ago, of ticks surviving eighteen years without a meal, clinging to their perch, patient as stone. She does not know about the forest. She does not know about the path, or the deer, or the season, or the slow rotation of constellations above her twig. Her entire universe consists of three signals. The first is the smell of butyric acid, which drifts up from the skin glands of passing mammals. When it arrives, she lets go and drops. The second is warmth, which guides her across fur to skin. The third is the texture of hairlessness, which triggers her to burrow, feed, and — her life's work complete — drop away, lay her eggs, and die.

Uexküll, a Baltic German zoologist who thought harder than anyone before him about how animals experience anything at all, found this story almost unbearable in its strangeness. Think of what the tick does not have. She has no eyes worth the name, no ears, no sense of the landscape around her. And yet nothing is missing, from inside. Her three signals arrive, in her lifetime, exactly as often as they need to. Her world is not a diminished version of ours. It is a different world entirely — complete, self-sufficient, closed like a bubble. Uexküll gave this bubble a name that has never quite escaped into everyday English, though it deserves to: the *Umwelt*.

A habitat is where an animal lives. An Umwelt is the world that lives in the animal — the specific, tailored slice of reality that an organism's senses carve out and its needs assemble into a home. Uexküll paired perception with action: every creature, he argued, runs a loop between what it can mark (its *Merkwelt*) and what it can do (its *Wirkwelt*), and the Umwelt is the product of that loop, forever. The same oak tree, he suggested, is many trees. For the beetle, it is a landscape of bark canyons. For the owl, a watchtower. For the fox, a wall of shade to move along. For the woodpecker, a pantry. None of these is the true tree. The tree-in-itself, whatever that might be, is never seen by anyone. What exists for each animal is the tree-as-it-matters-to-that-animal.

This was a quietly radical idea. Before Uexküll, the standard picture was that animals inhabit one world — the objective world, the one we see — but perceive it through inferior instruments. The dog gets a blurry version of the human show. Uexküll inverted this. There is no single show. There are billions of shows, running simultaneously, each edited for one audience. The Umwelt is not a poor copy of reality; it is a collaboration between reality and a body, and every body collaborates differently. Once you see this, you cannot unsee it. A walk in the woods becomes a walk through overlapping, mostly invisible nations.

Consider the bee. To us, a meadow flower is a splash of color. To a bee, many flowers are far more articulate: they carry patterns in ultraviolet light — dark central targets, radial landing strips — invisible to our eyes but blazing to a bee's, guiding her in to the nectar like runway lights. We only discovered these patterns by photographing flowers in UV, and the revelation was dizzying: the meadow we had walked through all our lives was plastered with signage we could not read. The flowers evolved their ultraviolet bulletins specifically for an audience with different eyes than ours. The bee's world and the flower's world have been negotiating with each other for a hundred million years, and neither negotiation needed us.

Or consider the elephant, whose social life has an entire channel we never suspected until 1984, when the acoustic researcher Katy Payne stood near a group of elephants at a zoo and felt a strange throbbing in the air, like standing in front of a large speaker at a distance. She realized the elephants were calling to each other in infrasound — rumbles pitched below the range of human hearing — that could travel for kilometers. Later work showed that these calls also travel through the ground, and that elephants can detect them through the fat pads of their feet, sometimes pressing their trunks to the earth, tilting forward onto their toes to listen. The seismic internet of elephants is invisible to us twice over: we cannot make the sounds, and we cannot receive them. Desert elephants in Namibia have been tracked making deliberate journeys toward rainstorms a hundred kilometers away, possibly by sensing the deep infrasonic rumble of thunder through their feet. They read weather through the earth.

The dog's Umwelt is built in a medium that is even harder for us to imagine, because we tend to assume sensing is mostly seeing. A dog has something like three hundred million olfactory receptors to our six million. But the deeper difference isn't quantity — it's that smell behaves like nothing in our sensory world. Light shows you the present. Odor lingers, diffuses, layers, fades. The concentration of a scent tells a story about time: strong here, faint there, gone over there. When a dog stops at a lamppost, she may be reading something like a newspaper, but a newspaper where every story is stamped with its age. Another dog passed at dawn, nervous; another last night, healthy; a female in season two days ago. The ethologist Alexandra Horowitz has argued that to a dog, smell is not merely a sense but a dimension — dogs perceive time the way we perceive space, spread out before them in gradients of intensity. A walk, for a dog, is time travel.

And then there is the bat, the animal Thomas Nagel made famous in philosophy by asking his famous question: what is it like to be one? Nagel's point, in his 1974 essay, was not that bats are mysterious because they live in caves and fly. It was that bats *perceive* the world largely through echolocation — a sense we do not merely lack but cannot even approximate by imagination. We can try to imagine seeing in sound, but what we'd be imagining is *seeing*, with sound substituted in, which is not the same thing. The bat doesn't translate echoes into pictures, any more than you translate light waves into sound. The echoes simply present the world — the shape of a moth's wing, the distance to a wall — directly, the way light presents the world to you. Nagel's conclusion was sobering: even if we learned every physical fact about bat sonar, down to the last neuron, we would still not know what echolocation is like *for the bat*. The subjective character of an experience cannot be reached from outside it. Every Umwelt is, from the outside, finally sealed.

Some Umwelten are so strange they destabilize our idea of a single self doing the perceiving. An octopus keeps two-thirds of its half-billion neurons not in its brain but in its arms, and those arms are semi-autonomous: a severed octopus arm will still reach and grasp, still recoil from a noxious stimulus. When an octopus explores a crevice, how much of the knowing is happening in the head, and how much in the arm that feels its way in? The animal's Umwelt may not be one bubble but a loose federation of eight. There's a further puzzle, unresolved: octopus eyes appear to be colorblind, and yet octopuses perform some of the most precise color-matching camouflage in nature. Some evidence suggests their skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins — that an octopus may, in some partial way, see with its body. We do not yet know how to describe that world, and the honest answer is that the octopus's Umwelt is one of the frontiers of our ignorance.

What I find most haunting about the Umwelt concept is that the bubbles hack each other. Uexküll marveled at the spider's web: the spider, which will never understand the fly's eyes, spins silk in gauges precisely tuned to be invisible to them — thin enough that the fly's vision cannot resolve the threads. The spider builds, without knowing, for the perceptual world of another creature. Evolution is full of these exploitations. The bolas spider releases a scent chemically identical to the sex pheromone of a female moth, and when a male moth comes fluttering toward the promise of a mate, the spider swings a sticky droplet on a thread and reels him in. The bee orchid grows flowers shaped and scented like a female bee, persuading male bees to attempt mating with them and carrying pollen away from the disappointment. No predator or flower *understands* its victim's Umwelt; it doesn't need to. Selection simply rewards any body that happens to mesh with another body's signals. The ecosystem is not just organisms eating organisms — it is worlds exploiting blind spots in other worlds, an arms race of bubbles.

There's a caution in the other direction, too. The mantis shrimp has been a mascot of sensory extravagance ever since people learned it possesses a dozen or more types of photoreceptor, against our measly three. Surely the mantis shrimp lives in a world of color we can't dream of! But when researchers finally tested them in 2014, the results were deflating and fascinating: mantis shrimp are surprisingly *bad* at telling colors apart — needing wavelength differences roughly ten times larger than the ones we need. The leading explanation is that they don't analyze color at all, in our sense; with so many pre-tuned receptors, they can glance at a wavelength and match it to a category instantly, trading precision for speed. The lesson is important: an Umwelt is not a sum of sensors. It is what an animal *does* with its signals. More channels do not mean a richer world. The world is built by use.

Which brings us, unavoidably, to ourselves — because the most difficult Umwelt to see is the one you're standing in. No creature misses the senses it doesn't have. Blindness to a channel is invisible from inside the bubble. It took centuries of science to discover, one by one, the worlds we are excluded from: the electric fields a shark reads through the jelly-filled pores in its snout, strong enough to detect the heartbeat of prey buried in sand; the magnetic fields that birds likely sense through molecules in their eyes, a compass overlaid on their vision; the polarized skylight that bees and ants navigate by. The entire visible spectrum — everything every human has ever seen — spans about one octave of electromagnetic radiation. The full spectrum, from radio to gamma rays, spans dozens of octaves. We live in a keyhole and call it daylight. And it's not just the physical channels. We are mesoscale creatures, evolved for middle-sized objects at middle speeds, which is why our intuitions about physics fail embarrassingly at the very small, the very fast, and the very large. Our Umwelt includes our language, our attention, our expectations — a bubble made not only of wavelengths but of habits of noticing.

Science, seen through Uexküll's lens, takes on a new character. It is the systematic craft of smuggling other worlds into ours. Telescopes and microscopes extend our existing senses; but a Geiger counter, a radio telescope, an MRI machine — these are different. They take signals that no animal on Earth can perceive and *translate* them into clicks, images, graphs — the dialects of the human Umwelt. Every instrument is an embassy, staffed full-time by a translator, mediating between our bubble and the realities outside it. Physics is the accumulated correspondence of these embassies. We have never seen reality naked. But by triangulating between many instruments' reports, we can sketch the shape of what must be out there beyond all bubbles — the an sich world Uexküll set aside — the way a sculptor who has never seen a face might nevertheless infer one from a thousand shadows.

The Umwelt concept also has a moral edge, and it's a practical one.
